title: Reading the paint
summary: What XRF, Raman and cross-sections can and can't tell you — then date five paintings by their newest material.

shots.title:
Reading
the paint.
shots.subtitle: What each instrument can — and **can't** — see.
shots.narration: Imaging shows where things are. Analysis says what they are. And knowing what an instrument cannot see matters as much as what it can.
X-ray fluorescence, now often portable, identifies chemical elements. Mercury in a red suggests vermilion — but it can't rule out other reds, including restorations or forgeries.

shots.heading: XRF's blind spots
items: Which layer an element sits in
Old smalt versus modern cobalt blue
shots.narration: Portable XRF can't identify individual light elements, almost entirely misses organic materials, can't say which layer it is reading, and has confused an old cobalt pigment with a modern one.

shots.text: **Raman** and cross-sections identify compounds and layers.
shots.narration: So examiners combine methods. Raman spectroscopy distinguishes compounds at high resolution, and a cross-section shows the layers under the microscope.

shots.text: Portable XRF misuse is **documented and widespread**.
shots.narration: A 2026 review warns that misuse of portable XRF in authentication is documented and widespread. Results must be read for the instrument used, and never over-interpreted.

shots.text: The newest material sets the **earliest possible date**.
shots.narration: Analysis gives you the materials; history gives you their dates. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century pigments are the classic markers, and the newest one present sets the terminus post quem.
Two real catches. Rutile titanium white, made from 1937, in Beltracchi's 'Campendonk' of 1914. And a plastic binder sold only since 1970 in fake 'Pollocks' — Pollock died in 1956.

shots.text: A modern pigment in a **retouching** dates the restoration, not the picture.
shots.narration: Two cautions. Old paintings get restored, so a modern pigment in a retouched area dates the repair. Check under UV, and sample the original paint.
And absence proves nothing. A forger who uses only period pigments gets a perfectly 'consistent' result. Materials can disprove a date; they can't confirm an author.

steps.title: Pigment dating lab
steps.brief: Five paintings, five analysis tables. For each, find the material that sets the earliest possible date of the **original** paint (a retouching doesn't count), then judge the claimed date. The last case is your capstone case file — save its result to your casebook.

items.name: Lead white
items.when: since antiquity; main white until the 19th century

cases.title: Dutch landscape
cases.context: A river landscape offered as a Dutch Golden Age work. Raman and XRF readings from four spots in the original paint:
cases.reveal: Prussian blue dates from 1704. In the original sky paint — not a retouching — it makes a 1650 date impossible.

cases.title: 'Campendonk' 1914
cases.context: 'Red Picture with Horses', sold at auction in 2006. The court record reports what the Doerner Institut found in 2008:
cases.reveal: Rutile titanium white was produced industrially only from 1937/38 — more than twenty years after the date on the picture. It was one of Beltracchi's forgeries.

cases.title: 'Pollock' drip
cases.claimLabel: sold as a Pollock — he died in 1956
cases.context: One of the drip paintings sold by John Re as Pollocks, analysed for the International Foundation for Art Research. The black paint's binder:
cases.reveal: ASA terpolymers have been commercially available only since 1970, after Pollock's death. Re pleaded guilty to wire fraud in 2014.

cases.title: River view 1875
cases.context: An Impressionist-style river view. One reading came from a small area that fluoresces dark under UV.
cases.reveal: The titanium white sits only in a retouching, so it dates the repair, not the picture. The original paint's newest materials date from the early 19th century — consistent with 1875, which proves nothing about who painted it.

cases.title: Case file 'HM 1631'
cases.context: The case-file portrait. All four samples come from the original paint, not from retouchings:
cases.reveal: Prussian blue in the original background paint puts the earliest possible date at 1704 — long after the date on the panel.

steps.title: Go deeper: Raman spectroscopy and forgery
steps.caption: A lecture by the chemist Robin Clark for SCI on using Raman spectroscopy to identify pigments and expose forgeries (about 70 minutes).

questions.prompt: XRF finds mercury in a red area. What can you conclude?
options: Probably vermilion or cinnabar — but other reds aren't ruled out
questions.explain: XRF identifies elements; the pigment is a deduction.

questions.prompt: Why might portable XRF miss a modern synthetic organic pigment?
options: Organic compounds almost completely elude XRF
questions.explain: Use Raman, FTIR or chromatography for organics.

questions.prompt: Titanium white turns up only in an area that fluoresces dark under UV. What does it date?
questions.explain: Later paint on top of the varnish shows dark in UV; a modern pigment there dates the repair.

questions.prompt: What did the Doerner Institut find in the 'Campendonk'?
questions.explain: A form of titanium white produced industrially only from 1937/38.
